title: Deaths of local musicians, saxophonists and tenor man Cliff Curry at Keesler Field
summary: DeDroit and Allen talk about the death of local saxophonists, and DeDroit describes his long-time tenor player Cliff Curry and singing at Keesler Field.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: And Elri Mazur died, I just heard that last night. Elri Mazur? I just heard that last night.

I used that, Elri. When you're in 40 years you have a lot of turnover. Elri's a good musician. Not great, but good. Bouchon was better than he was supposed to be, you know? But he didn't care. He was selling pies or something. What did he have, a catering business? He had a bar business.
He went in the bar business, he had a bar room. Oh no, he had something.
The trouble is that the good man, you know, goes to the head sometimes and can't handle them.
Well nobody ever gave us to do so much credit as a saxophone player except the musicians.

Well I'll tell you, he was a good tenor man. When he played the chorus he played the last thing. Grab that. But I didn't use it. I had the same tenor man for 13 years. He was a scat singer. I used to sing numbers like, save the Confederate money to South the Rise again. I used to do that at Keishler Field. The Southern, it was a competition between the Northern officers and the Southern officers. You'd get up and cheer and wave. You ever hear that number, save the Confederate money?
I've heard of it, yeah. What year was that? Do you remember what year about that was?

Oh, that was in my, I'd say, mid-fifties. This tenor man, his name is Cliff Curry, he was a major at the Board of Application. He was never any hired as a sergeant when he was in the Army, but he had such an important job. So he could give orders and be a major. He was a major. When he was a graduate of Springville, he was a certified public accountant, you know what I mean? He was not out of the ordinary, a talented fellow, nice looking. Used to dye his hair. One night he came there with a steel blue, like a woman, you know what women have? I said, are you nuts? You're going to think you're good. I said, don't come on the next job in that hair. So he came back with black, he was gray. And he looked good with gray hair. Some people do. Did you ever have any contact with Huey Long?
